The word dispatch has a few related meanings. They all share a common thread: something being sent, done, or dealt with — quickly and purposefully.
Meaning 1: An Official Message or Report Sent Quickly

This is the most common meaning. A dispatch is a piece of written communication — a message, report, or piece of news — that is sent urgently and officially from one place or person to another.

Think of it this way: not every message is a dispatch. A casual text to a friend is not a dispatch. But when a war correspondent on a battlefield writes a report and rushes it back to their newspaper, that report is a dispatch. When a military commander sends an urgent written update to headquarters, that is a dispatch.

The word carries a sense of importance and urgency. It is used in formal, official, or serious contexts — journalism, military, government, and diplomacy.

Examples:

  • "The journalist sent a dispatch from the war zone, describing the scene in detail."
  • "The general received a dispatch from the front lines."
  • "News dispatches arrived from around the world."

A collection of such messages can also be called dispatches (plural), and you'll often see expressions like "mentioned in dispatches" — a British military term meaning someone was officially noted in battle reports for doing something brave or outstanding.
Meaning 2: The Act of Sending Something or Someone Off

A dispatch can also refer to the act of sending someone or something away to a destination, usually with a specific mission or purpose.

Here, the word describes the moment or process of sending — not the message itself, but the action.

Examples:

  • "The dispatch of soldiers to the border happened at dawn."
  • "The dispatch of the relief packages was delayed due to bad weather."
  • "After the dispatch of the rescue team, the coordinator waited for news."

Notice that in this sense, it is often used with the preposition "of" — the dispatch of something/someone.
Meaning 3: Speed and Efficiency in Getting Something Done

This is an older and more formal meaning, but you will still encounter it in books, literature, and formal writing. In this sense, dispatch means promptness, speed, and efficiency — the quality of handling something quickly and without wasting time.

When someone does a task "with dispatch," it means they handled it swiftly and effectively.

Examples:

  • "The surgeon completed the procedure with great dispatch."
  • "She handled all her responsibilities with admirable dispatch."
  • "The matter was dealt with dispatch — no time was wasted."

This usage is not common in everyday conversation today, but it's important to recognise it when you read it.
Meaning 4: The Act of Killing Quickly (Formal / Rare)

This is a rare and formal sense, but worth knowing. A dispatch can refer to the act of killing someone or something quickly, especially to end suffering or in a military context. You might encounter this in older literature or formal reports.

Example:

  • "The hunter performed a swift dispatch of the injured animal."

You are unlikely to use this meaning in everyday life, but recognizing it will prevent confusion when you encounter it.
Putting It All Together: The Common Thread

All four meanings of dispatch share the same underlying idea:

Something is handled, sent, or dealt with — purposefully, officially, and usually quickly.

Whether it's a message being sent urgently, troops being deployed, a task being completed efficiently, or a life being ended swiftly — in every case, there is a sense of decisive, prompt action.
Common Phrases and Contexts to Remember

• "A dispatch from [place]" → a news report or message from that location
  • "With dispatch" → quickly and efficiently
  • "The dispatch of [something]" → the act of sending something off
  • "News dispatch" → a piece of news sent by a reporter
  • "Mentioned in dispatches" → formally noted in official military reports for bravery
